key_insight: Factually accurate peer-to-peer health advice can still be unsafe, so alignment with medical consensus is not a reliable proxy for health risk.
clinical_relevance: For online health moderation and triage, systems should assess both factual correctness and potential behavioral harm rather than relying on accuracy alone.
method: Analyzed 704 health narratives (699 classified) using two separate scores: Narrative Truth Distance and Narrative Risk Score.
Compared epistemic divergence vs. health risk and mapped content into four classification quadrants.
Evaluated benchmark behavior on 437 expert-labeled posts with 127 misinformation instances.
evidence_signal: The two scores shared only 4.9% variance (r = 0.222), and 39.6% of narratives fell into off-diagonal cases that single-axis fact-checking would mis-handle.
watch_item: The framework is promising for moderation design, but quadrant-based decisions may still need expert review because benchmark labels for factual accuracy do not capture real-world behavioral risk.
paper_title: The Online Health Safety Gap: Consensus Alignment Does Not Imply Safety in Peer-to-Peer Health Narratives.
